title: Backend Programming
description: Understand servers, HTTP, APIs, validation, databases, security, and the steps required to build a small JSON API.

paths.title: Server Foundations
paths.description: Learn request-response flow, routes, databases, and backend responsibilities.

paths.title: Build Your First API
paths.description: Plan, build, validate, test, and connect a small Node.js JSON API.

paths.title: Production Backend Essentials
paths.description: Study permissions, secrets, transactions, retries, and production readiness.

cards.title: What the backend is
cards.prompt: The backend is the part of an application that runs away from the user interface and manages trusted application logic.
cards.content: A backend can validate requests, enforce permissions, read and write databases, process files, send messages, and coordinate other services. It usually runs on a server or cloud platform.

cards.title: A server receives requests
cards.prompt: A server waits for a client request, performs work, and returns a response.
cards.content: The client may be a browser, mobile app, another server, or command-line tool. The request and response follow a protocol, commonly HTTP for web applications.

cards.title: HTTP messages carry method, path, headers, and body
cards.prompt: These parts tell the server what action is requested and what information accompanies it.
cards.content: For example, POST /api/tasks may include JSON in the request body. The response includes a status code, headers, and usually a JSON body.

cards.title: Choose the retrieval method
cards.prompt: Which HTTP method is normally used to retrieve a resource without changing it?

question.explanation: GET is intended for reading a resource and should not create a state-changing side effect.

cards.title: Routes connect URLs to handlers
cards.prompt: A backend route matches a request method and path, then calls code that handles the request.
cards.content: GET /api/facts and POST /api/facts can share a path but perform different work because their HTTP methods differ.

cards.title: Databases preserve application data
cards.prompt: A database stores information beyond the lifetime of one request or one server process.
cards.content: Relational databases organize data into related tables and use SQL. Document databases store document-shaped records. The choice should follow the data model and query needs.

cards.title: Separate temporary and persistent data
cards.prompt: Which item should normally be stored in a database rather than only in a local variable?

options: A loop counter used during one request
question.explanation: User accounts must remain available after the process restarts and across many requests.

cards.title: Backend responsibility check
cards.prompt: Use the backend for operations that require trust, shared state, or secret credentials.
cards.content: Do not place database passwords, private API keys, or authorization decisions in browser code because users can inspect and modify it.
items: Return clear status codes and error messages.

cards.title: Plan your first API
cards.prompt: Define one small resource and its operations before writing server code.
cards.content: A focused first API is easier to test. This learning path uses a facts resource with read and create operations.
steps: Define POST /api/facts to create one fact.
Decide the required fields: topic and statement.
Define success and validation error responses.
Write sample request and response JSON.

cards.title: Create a minimal Node.js server
cards.prompt: Node can run JavaScript outside the browser and includes a built-in HTTP server module.
cards.content: This server listens on port 3000 and returns JSON. It is intentionally small so the request-response cycle is visible.

cards.title: Route a GET request
cards.prompt: Inspect the request method and URL before choosing a response.
cards.content: The route returns an array of facts. Unknown routes fall through to a 404 response so clients are not given a misleading success result.

cards.title: Request bodies arrive as a stream
cards.prompt: A server may receive the body in multiple chunks rather than as one ready-made string.
cards.content: Frameworks often parse JSON automatically, but understanding streams explains body-size limits, partial uploads, and why parsing can fail.

cards.title: Read and parse JSON
cards.prompt: Collect request chunks, enforce a size limit, then parse the completed JSON string.
cards.content: The limit reduces accidental or malicious oversized requests. JSON.parse can throw, so production code should catch parsing errors and return status 400.

cards.title: Validation rejects malformed input early
cards.prompt: Validation checks whether incoming data has the expected shape, type, length, and allowed values.
cards.content: A request can contain valid JSON but still be invalid for the application. For example, topic may be missing or statement may be an empty string.

cards.title: Choose the validation response
cards.prompt: A client sends valid JSON but omits a required field. Which status code is a reasonable response?

question.explanation: A 400 response tells the client that the submitted request does not satisfy the endpoint requirements.

cards.title: Return a created resource
cards.prompt: After validating input, create a server-owned id and return status 201.
cards.content: The server controls the id instead of trusting a client-provided value. A real application would persist the record in a database before returning success.

cards.title: Test the first API
cards.prompt: Test both successful requests and expected failures.
cards.content: An API test should verify the status code and response body. Failure-path tests often catch more important defects than another happy-path example.
items: POST with valid fields returns status 201.
The created fact appears in a later GET response.
Invalid JSON does not crash the server.

cards.title: Connect the frontend to the API
cards.prompt: Replace hard-coded browser data with an HTTP request to the backend.
cards.content: The frontend and backend must agree on the URL, request method, JSON fields, and possible error responses. This agreement is the API contract.
steps: Open the frontend from an allowed origin.
Show a loading state while waiting.
Render the returned JSON on success.
Show a useful message for non-success responses.
Confirm the browser Network panel shows the expected request.

cards.title: Authentication and authorization are different
cards.prompt: Authentication determines who is making the request. Authorization determines what that identity is allowed to do.
cards.content: A signed-in user may be authenticated but still lack permission to delete another user’s data. Backends must enforce both checks on every protected operation.

cards.title: Passwords should be hashed, not encrypted for retrieval
cards.prompt: A backend should store a slow, salted password hash rather than the original password.
cards.content: During sign-in, the submitted password is hashed and compared using a password-hashing function such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt. Plaintext passwords must never be logged or stored.

cards.title: Transactions protect multi-step database changes
cards.prompt: A transaction groups related database operations so they either all succeed or all fail.
cards.content: For example, transferring a balance requires subtracting from one account and adding to another. Committing only one operation would corrupt the data.

cards.title: Idempotency makes retries safer
cards.prompt: An idempotent operation can be repeated without creating an unintended additional effect.
cards.content: GET, PUT, and DELETE are designed to be idempotent when implemented correctly. For payment-like POST operations, an idempotency key can prevent duplicate processing after a retry.

cards.title: Keep secrets on the server
cards.prompt: Where should a private database password be stored for a deployed backend?

options: In the deployment platform’s secret or environment-variable system
question.explanation: Deployment secrets should be injected into the server environment and excluded from browser bundles and source control.

cards.title: Production backend baseline
cards.prompt: A deployable backend needs more than working route handlers.
cards.content: Start simple, then add controls based on actual risk and scale. Observability and safe failure behavior are part of the product.
items: Set request size and rate limits.
Use structured logs without sensitive values.
Add health checks and graceful shutdown.
Back up persistent data and test restoration.
